body.heading: A delivery plants cannot make themselves
paragraphs: Pollination is the transfer of pollen — a flower's male cells — to the female part of a flower, where it can fertilise an egg cell and start a seed. Plants cannot walk to each other, so they need a courier, and evolution has hired two main ones: animals and the wind.

Animal-pollinated flowers advertise. They offer nectar, a sugary drink, and pollen itself as food, and they signal with colour, scent and patterns — including ultraviolet guides visible to bees but not to us.

body.heading: How a bee becomes a courier
paragraphs: A bee visiting a flower for nectar brushes against its pollen-producing anthers. Pollen grains stick to the bee's hairy body — static electricity helps them jump across — and when the bee visits the next flower, some grains rub off onto its sticky stigma. Delivery complete.

Wind-pollinated plants play a numbers game instead. Grasses, maize and many trees make huge amounts of light, dusty pollen and release it to the air, trusting the wind to land a few grains on the right flower. Their flowers are usually small and dull — no advertising needed.

body.heading: Dinner depends on it
paragraphs: About a third of the food people eat benefits from insect pollination: apples, almonds, strawberries, coffee and many more crops set far more fruit when bees visit. Farmers near orchards sometimes rent hives during blossom season purely as a delivery service.

The partnership is ancient and precise. Some orchids are pollinated by a single insect species, shaped over millions of years to fit each other like a lock and key. When pollinators decline, the effects travel the same route in reverse, from flower to fruit to the animals that eat both.

takeaway: Pollination delivers pollen to a flower's stigma so seeds can form; insects carry it for food rewards, while wind-pollinated plants release clouds of light pollen.
